heading_en: Men rise from one ambition to another
thesis: Men climb from one ambition to the next: first they seek only security from offense, then they offend others; in defending themselves from fear they make themselves feared, so republics dissolve as each side oppresses the other.
thesis_quote: mentre che gli uomini cercono di non temere, cominciono a fare temere altrui; e quella ingiuria che gli scacciano da loro, la pongono sopra un altro

propositions.statement: Ambitious citizens first secure themselves against offense by acquiring friends through apparently honest means—money and protection—which deceives everyone and prevents any remedy.
propositions.quote: cercono, per poter fare questo, amicizie; e quelle acquistano per vie in apparenza oneste, o con sovvenire di danari, o con difenderli da’ potenti

propositions.statement: Once such a citizen has grown great unopposed, the city must either crush him at risk of sudden ruin or slide into open servitude.
propositions.quote: bisogna, o cercare di spegnerlo con pericolo d’una subita rovina, o, lasciandolo fare, entrare in una servitù manifesta

propositions.statement: A republic should order itself so as to watch that citizens cannot do evil under the shadow of good, and that their reputation helps rather than harms liberty.
propositions.quote: una republica intra gli ordini suoi debbe avere questo, di vegghiare che i suoi cittadini, sotto ombra di bene non possino fare male

episodes.description: After the plebs recovered its liberty from the decemvirs, new tumults arose: young nobles began injuring the quiet plebs and the tribunes could offer few remedies, each side oppressing the other in defending its liberty.
episodes.quote: stando la plebe quieta intra i termini suoi, cominciarono i giovani nobili a ingiuriarla; ed i Tribuni vi potevon fare pochi rimedi

notes: Machiavelli explicitly paraphrases Livy's words (Livy 3.65: 'cavendo ne metuant, homines metuendos ultro se efficiunt') and quotes Sallust's sentence placed in Caesar's mouth ('quod omnia mala exempla bonis initiis orta sunt').

heading_en: Men deceive themselves in generalities, not in particulars
thesis: Though men deceive themselves in general matters, they do not deceive themselves in particulars: the people, judging specific men and cases, corrects errors it makes when judging in the abstract.
thesis_quote: gli uomini nelle cose generali s’ingannono assai, nelle particulari non tanto

propositions.statement: Peoples deceive themselves generally in judging things and events, but once they come to know them in particular the deception vanishes.
propositions.quote: Ingannonsi, oltra di questo, i popoli generalmente nel giudicare le cose e gli accidenti di esse; le quali, dipoi si conoscono particularmente, mancano di tale inganno

propositions.statement: A prudent man should never flee popular judgment in particular matters such as the distribution of offices and dignities, for there the people is rarely deceived.
propositions.quote: mai un uomo prudente non debba fuggire il giudicio populare nelle cose particulari, circa le distribuzioni de’ gradi e delle dignità

propositions.statement: When a generality deceives the people, their eyes can quickly be opened by finding a way to make them descend to particulars.
propositions.quote: si può fare tosto aprire gli occhi a’ popoli, trovando modo, veggendo che uno generale gl’inganna, ch’egli abbino a discendere a’ particulari

episodes.description: When tribunes with consular power open to plebeians were first elected, the Roman people, though able to choose all plebeians, elected all nobles.
episodes.quote: venendosi alla creazione di questi Tribuni, e potendosi creare tutti plebei, furono dal Popolo romano creati tutti nobili

episodes.description: After Cannae, Pacuvius Calavius in Capua reconciled the plebs with the Senate by locking up the senators and inviting the people to replace each one, whereupon the people found every proposed substitute unworthy.
episodes.quote: trovandosi in quel tempo nel supremo magistrato Pacuvio Calano, e conoscendo il pericolo che portava quella città di tumultuare

episodes.description: After 1494 Florentine populars blamed ambitious magnates for the city's disorders, but whenever one of them reached the supreme magistracy and saw things closely, he changed his mind—whence the proverb that they had one mind in the piazza and another in the palazzo.
episodes.quote: Dopo il 1494, sendo stati i principi della città cacciati da Firenze, e non vi essendo alcuno governo ordinato

notes: Two verbatim Latin quotations from Livy 4.6 appear in the chapter. The Capua episode corresponds to Livy 23.2-4, outside the books in the local Livy corpus (1-10), so no candidate is given.

thesis: He who does not want a magistracy given to a vile or wicked man should have it requested either by someone exceedingly vile and wicked or by someone exceedingly noble and good, so that the people is shamed into choosing well.
thesis_quote: Chi vuole che uno magistrato non sia dato a uno vile o a uno cattivo, lo facci domandare o a uno troppo vile e troppo cattivo o a uno troppo nobile e troppo buono

propositions.statement: Having a base candidate stand shames the plebs into not giving the office; having a most reputed man stand shames it into not taking the office for itself.
propositions.quote: Questo ultimo modo faceva che la plebe si vergognava a darlo; quel primo faceva che la si vergognava a torlo

propositions.statement: The people, though it deceives itself in generalities, does not deceive itself in particulars.
propositions.quote: il popolo, se s’inganna de’ generali, de’ particulari non s’inganna

episodes.description: When the Senate feared that tribunes with consular power would go to plebeians, it either had the most reputed Romans stand for the office or corrupted some ignoble plebeian to stand alongside the better plebeian candidates.
episodes.quote: Quando il Senato dubitava che i Tribuni con potestà consolare non fussero fatti d’uomini plebei, teneva uno de’ due modi

notes: Very short chapter; a corollary of chapter 47 on electoral practice.

heading_en: Servile-born cities can hardly order themselves free
thesis: If cities born free like Rome struggle to find laws that keep them free, cities born in servitude, like Florence, find it nearly impossible ever to order themselves so as to live civilly and quietly.
thesis_quote: se quelle città che hanno avuto il principio loro libero, e che per sé medesimo si è retto, come Roma, hanno difficultà grande a trovare leggi buone per mantenerle libere

propositions.statement: Cities whose beginnings were immediately servile face not merely difficulty but impossibility in ever ordering themselves to live civilly and quietly.
propositions.quote: quelle città che hanno avuto il principio loro immediate servo, abbino, non che difficultà, ma impossibilità a ordinarsi mai in modo che le possino vivere civilmente e quietamente

propositions.statement: An orderer of a republic must examine into whose hands he places the authority over the blood of its citizens.
propositions.quote: intra le altre cose che si hanno a considerare da uno ordinatore d’una republica è esaminare nelle mani di quali uomini ei ponga l’autorità del sangue contro de’ suoi cittadini

propositions.statement: When capital authority is placed in the hands of a few citizens, the few are always ministers of the few and of the most powerful.
propositions.quote: i pochi furono sempre ministri de’ pochi, e de’ più potenti

episodes.description: Rome created the censors to guard its morals, first for five-year terms; the dictator Mamercus by a new law reduced the office to eighteen months, and the offended censors expelled him from the Senate without remedy.
episodes.quote: fu corretto dalla prudenza di Mamerco dittatore, il quale per nuova legge ridusse detto magistrato a diciotto mesi

episodes.description: Florence, born subject to the Roman Empire and long governed by others, has managed itself for the two hundred years of true memory without ever attaining a state that could truly be called a republic.
episodes.quote: è ita maneggiandosi, per dugento anni che si ha di vera memoria, sanza avere mai avuto stato, per il quale la possa veramente essere chiamata republica

episodes.description: Venice guards against corrupt capital justice with the Ten who punish any citizen without appeal, reinforced by the Quarantia and the Council of the Pregadi to curb the powerful.
episodes.quote: ha dieci cittadini, che, sanza appello, possono punire ogni cittadino

notes: Mentions the lawgiving of Romulus, Numa, Tullus Hostilius, Servius and the decemvirs as background. 'La istoria' is invoked but Livy is not named.

heading_en: No council or magistrate should be able to halt the city's business
thesis: No single council or magistrate should be able to halt the public actions of a city: whoever holds a necessary deliberation must be compelled to perform it, or another must be empowered to perform it in his place.
thesis_quote: mai si debbe ordinare in una città, che i pochi possino tenere alcuna diliberazione di quelle che ordinariamente sono necessarie a mantenere la republica

propositions.statement: If a council or magistrate is given a necessary public function, one must either impose a necessity that it be done in any case or order that, if he will not do it, another can and must.
propositions.quote: conviene o imporgli una necessità perché ci l’abbia a fare in ogni modo, o ordinare, quando non la voglia fare egli, che la possa e debba fare uno altro

propositions.statement: The tribunate was useful not only to check the ambition the powerful used against the plebs, but also that which they used among themselves.
propositions.quote: il quale non era solo utile a frenare l’ambizione che i potenti usavano contro alla Plebe, ma quella ancora ch’egli usavano infra loro

episodes.description: The disunited consuls Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus and Gnaeus Julius Mento halted all actions of the republic and refused to name a dictator, until the Senate resorted to the tribunes, who forced the consuls to obey.
episodes.quote: il Senato, non avendo altro rimedio, ricorse allo aiuto de’ Tribuni; i quali, con l’autorità del Senato, sforzarono i Consoli a ubbidire

episodes.description: The Venetian Great Council sometimes refused out of disdain to elect successors to magistrates at home and abroad, until prudent citizens passed a law that no magistracy should ever fall vacant until successors were chosen.
episodes.quote: fecero una legge, che tutti i magistrati che sono o fusseno dentro e fuori della città, mai vacassero, se non quando fussono fatti gli scambi e i successori loro

heading_en: Appear liberal in what necessity compels
thesis: A republic or prince should make a show of doing out of liberality what necessity in any case compels, thereby earning gratitude for the unavoidable.
thesis_quote: Una republica o uno principe debbe mostrare di fare per liberalità quello a che la necessità lo constringe

propositions.statement: Prudent men always make a merit of their actions, even those that necessity would have compelled them to do in any case.
propositions.quote: Gli uomini prudenti si fanno grado delle cose sempre e in ogni loro azione, ancora che la necessità gli constringesse a farle in ogni modo

episodes.description: The Roman Senate, needing longer campaigns and sieges, decreed public pay for soldiers who had served at their own expense, presenting necessity as a gift; the plebs rejoiced, the tribunes failed to discredit it, and the Senate taxed the nobility first and most heavily.
episodes.quote: diliberò, che si desse il soldo del publico agli uomini che militavano, essendo consueti militare del loro proprio

heading_en: Preempt the roads by which a rising man gains power
thesis: The safest and least scandalous way to repress the insolence of one rising to power in a republic is to preoccupy in advance the ways by which he climbs to that power.
thesis_quote: non si può in una republica, e massime in quelle che sono corrotte, con miglior modo, meno scandoloso e più facile, opporsi all’ambizione di alcuno cittadino, che preoccupandogli quelle vie

propositions.statement: Had Cosimo's rivals adopted his own style of favoring the people, they would have disarmed him without tumult or violence.
propositions.quote: se quegli cittadini che gareggiavano seco avessero preso lo stile suo, di favorire il popolo, gli venivano, sanza tumulto e sanza violenza, a trarre di mano quelle armi di che egli si valeva più

propositions.statement: In every course of action men should weigh its defects and dangers, and not adopt it when it holds more danger than utility.
propositions.quote: Debbono, pertanto, gli uomini in ogni partito considerare i difetti ed i pericoli di quello, e non gli prendere, quando vi sia più del pericoloso che dell’utile

episodes.description: Cosimo de' Medici's adversaries expelled him from Florence instead of preempting the popular favor on which his power rested, a worse course that led to their ruin.
episodes.quote: Il quale modo se fusse stato usato contro a Cosimo de’ Medici, sarebbe stato miglior partito assai per gli suoi avversari, che cacciarlo da Firenze

episodes.description: Piero Soderini built his reputation in Florence solely by favoring the generality of citizens; his envious rivals could more safely have taken over his methods than opposed him at the republic's peril.
episodes.quote: Piero Soderini si aveva fatto riputazione nella città di Firenze con questo solo, di favorire l’universale

episodes.description: Cicero, seeking to strip Mark Antony of his soldiers, urged the Senate to raise up Octavian against him; instead Octavian allied with Antony, destroying the party of the optimates.
episodes.quote: Tullio, per torgli questi soldati, confortò il Senato a dare riputazione ad Ottaviano, e mandarlo con Irzio e Pansa consoli contro a Marc’Antonio

notes: The Cicero-Octavian episode belongs to the lost later books of Livy/other sources; no candidate possible from the Livy 1-10 corpus.

heading_en: The people, deceived by a false good, desires its own ruin
thesis: The people, deceived by a false appearance of good, often desires its own ruin, and is easily moved by great hopes and brave promises, while courses that look timid or losing cannot be sold to it even when salvation lies hidden in them.
thesis_quote: il popolo molte volte, ingannato da una falsa immagine di bene, disidera la rovina sua

propositions.statement: Proposals that show gain on their face, or that seem spirited, are always easy to persuade a multitude of, even when loss or the republic's ruin lies hidden beneath.
propositions.quote: quando nelle cose che si mettono innanzi al popolo, si vede guadagno, ancora che vi sia nascosto sotto perdita; e quando e’ pare animoso, ancora che vi sia nascosto sotto la rovina della republica, sempre sarà facile persuaderlo alla moltitudine

propositions.statement: There is no easier way to ruin a republic where the people has authority than to set it upon bold enterprises.
propositions.quote: non è la più facile via a fare rovinare una republica dove il popolo abbia autorità, che metterla in imprese gagliarde

propositions.statement: Having presupposed victory, the people blames defeat not on fortune or the commander's weakness but on his malice and ignorance, and kills, imprisons, or banishes him.
propositions.quote: avendosi il popolo presupposto la vittoria, come ei viene la perdita, non ne accusa né la fortuna né la impotenzia di chi ha governato, ma la malvagità e ignoranza sua

episodes.description: After the capture of Veii the Roman plebs embraced the opinion that half of Rome should migrate there, and nearly came to arms against the Senate until the reverence of grave citizens restrained it.
episodes.quote: entrò nel popolo romano un’opinione, che fosse cosa utile per la città di Roma, che la metà de’ Romani andasse ad abitare a Veio

episodes.description: Fabius Maximus could not persuade the Roman people that proceeding slowly against Hannibal was useful, since the people judged that course cowardly, and his master of horse was given authority to fight.
episodes.quote: non poteva persuadere al Popolo romano, che fusse utile a quella Republica procedere lentamente in quella guerra, e sostenere sanza azzuffarsi l’impeto d’Annibale

episodes.description: Varro was made consul only for having promised in all the public places of Rome to crush Hannibal, from which followed the battle and rout of Cannae and almost the ruin of Rome.
episodes.quote: fece di poi consule Varrone, non per altri suoi meriti che per avere, per tutte le piazze e tutti i luoghi publici di Roma, promesso di rompere Annibale

episodes.description: Marcus Centenius Penula, a most vile man, obtained from the wary Senate authority to raise volunteers against Hannibal and was routed and killed with all his followers.
episodes.quote: venne in Senato Marco Centenio Penula, uomo vilissimo (nondimanco aveva avuto qualche grado nella milizia)

episodes.description: In Athens the grave and prudent Nicias could not dissuade the people from assaulting Sicily, a decision taken against the wise that brought Athens' total ruin.
episodes.quote: non potette mai Nicia, uomo gravissimo e prudentissimo, persuadere a quel Popolo che non fusse bene andare a assaltare Sicilia

episodes.description: Scipio, made consul and desiring the province of Africa while promising Carthage's ruin, threatened to take the proposal to the people when the Senate balked on Fabius Maximus' advice.
episodes.quote: Scipione, quando fu fatto consolo, e che desiderava la provincia di Africa, promettendo al tutto la rovina di Cartagine

episodes.description: Venice, assaulted by many enemies, could not bring itself to buy off any of them by restoring what it had taken, before its ruin came.
episodes.quote: assaltati da tanti inimici, non poterono prendere partito di guadagnarsene alcuno con la restituzione delle cose tolte ad altri

episodes.description: On Ercole Bentivoglio's brave promises the Florentine people decreed the camp against Pisa despite wise citizens' blame; after the failure Antonio Giacomini fell into such popular disgrace that he survived only by the humanity of those in power.
episodes.quote: andarono a campo a Pisa la quale impresa fu diliberata dal popolo in su le promesse gagliarde di messere Ercole

notes: Cites Dante's De Monarchia ('Viva la sua morte! e Muoia la sua vita!'). Fabius/Varro/Cannae (Livy 22), Centenius (Livy 25) and Scipio (Livy 28) fall outside the Livy 1-10 corpus, so no candidates are given.

heading_en: A grave man can restrain an excited multitude
thesis: Nothing is so apt to restrain an excited multitude as the reverence inspired by some grave man of authority who comes before it.
thesis_quote: veruna cosa è tanto atta a frenare una moltitudine concitata, quanto è la riverenzia di qualche uomo grave e di autorità, che se le faccia incontro

propositions.statement: Whoever commands an army or finds himself in a city where tumult arises should present himself with the greatest grace and honor, wearing the insignia of his rank to make himself more revered.
propositions.quote: quello che è preposto a uno esercito, o quello che si trova in una città, dove nascesse tumulto debba rappresentarsi in su quello con maggiore grazia e più onorevolmente che può

propositions.statement: There is no firmer or more necessary remedy to restrain an excited multitude than the presence of a man who by his bearing appears and is worthy of reverence.
propositions.quote: e’ non è il più fermo né il più necessario rimedio a frenare una moltitudine concitata, che la presenzia d’uno uomo che per presenzia paia e sia riverendo

episodes.description: When the armed Florentine mob of the Arrabbiati came to sack Pagolantonio Soderini's house, his brother Francesco, bishop of Volterra, put on his most honorable robes and episcopal rochet and halted them with his presence and words.
episodes.quote: messosi i più onorevoli panni indosso, e di sopra il roccetto episcopale, si fece incontro a quegli armati, e con la presenzia e con le parole gli fermò

episodes.description: The Roman plebs obstinately embraced the plan of migrating to Veii, judging it useful and not seeing the harm beneath, until the Senate restrained its fury with grave and revered men.
episodes.quote: con quanta ostinazione la plebe romana accettava quel partito d’andare a Veio, perché lo giudicava utile, né vi conosceva, sotto, il danno vi era

notes: Quotes Virgil, Aeneid 1.151-152 ('Tum pietate gravem ac meritis...'). Continues the Veii-migration text discussed in chapter 53.

heading_en: Where equality, no principality; where inequality, no republic
thesis: Public affairs are easily managed where the multitude is not corrupt; where equality reigns no principality can be made, and where great inequality reigns no republic can be made.
thesis_quote: dove è equalità, non si può fare principato; e dove la non è, non si può fare republica

propositions.statement: Gentlemen are those who live idly and abundantly off the revenues of their possessions without any care for cultivation or other necessary labor; they are pernicious in every republic.
propositions.quote: gentiluomini sono chiamati quelli che oziosi vivono delle rendite delle loro possessioni abbondantemente, sanza avere cura alcuna o di coltivazione o di altra necessaria fatica a vivere

propositions.statement: Whoever wants to make a republic where there are many gentlemen cannot do so unless he first extinguishes them all.
propositions.quote: colui che vuole fare dove sono assai gentiluomini una republica, non la può fare se prima non gli spegne tutti

propositions.statement: Where the matter is so corrupt that laws do not suffice to restrain it, a greater force must be ordered along with them: a kingly hand with absolute and excessive power to bridle the excessive ambition and corruption of the powerful.
propositions.quote: dove è tanto la materia corrotta che le leggi non bastano a frenarla, vi bisogna ordinare insieme con quelle maggior forza; la quale è una mano regia

episodes.description: To satisfy Camillus' vow of a tenth of the Veientine spoils to Apollo, the Senate issued an edict that each man present publicly a tenth of his plunder, trusting wholly in the plebs' goodness.
episodes.quote: fece il Senato uno editto, che ciascuno dovessi rappresentare in publico la decima parte di quello ch’egli aveva predato

episodes.description: In the German republics citizens assess their own taxes, swearing an oath and throwing into a chest what conscience tells them they owe, with no witness but the payer—proof of surviving ancient goodness.
episodes.quote: preso prima il giuramento di pagare la conveniente somma, getta in una cassa a ciò diputata quello che secondo la conscienza sua gli pare dovere pagare

episodes.description: In Tuscany three republics—Florence, Siena and Lucca—have long existed in a small space because the province has no lords of castles and few or no gentlemen, but great equality.
episodes.quote: si vede in poco spazio di terreno state lungamente tre republiche, Firenze, Siena e Lucca

episodes.description: Venice does not contradict the rule, for its gentlemen are such more in name than in fact, their wealth resting on trade and movables, with no castles or jurisdiction over men.
episodes.quote: i gentiluomini in quella Republica sono più in nome che in fatto; perché loro non hanno grandi entrate di possessioni

notes: The German-cities episode concerns contemporary Germany (1500s); the period label 'contemporary-italy' is used here for Machiavelli's own era. The tithe edict appears in Livy 5.23 (also treated in 5.25).

heading_en: Great events are preceded by signs and prophecies
thesis: Before great events befall a city or province, signs come that prognosticate them, or men who predict them—whether by diviners, revelations, prodigies, or other celestial signs.
thesis_quote: mai non venne alcuno grave accidente in una città o in una provincia, che non sia stato, o da indovini o da rivelazioni o da prodigi o da altri segni celesti, predetto

propositions.statement: After such signs, extraordinary and new things always befall the provinces.
propositions.quote: sempre dopo tali accidenti sopravvengono cose istraordinarie e nuove alle provincie

propositions.statement: Perhaps, as some philosophers hold, the air is full of intelligences which foresee future things by natural powers and, out of compassion, warn men with such signs so they may prepare their defenses.
propositions.quote: potrebbe essere che, sendo questo aere, come vuole alcuno filosofo, pieno di intelligenze, le quali per naturali virtù preveggendo le cose future, ed avendo compassione agli uomini, acciò si possino preparare alle difese, gli avvertiscono con simili segni

episodes.description: Friar Girolamo Savonarola predicted the coming of King Charles VIII of France into Italy before it happened.
episodes.quote: sa ciascuno quanto da frate Girolamo Savonerola fosse predetta innanzi la venuta del re Carlo VIII di Francia in Italia

episodes.description: Throughout Tuscany it was said that men-at-arms were heard and seen in the air above Arezzo, fighting one another.
episodes.quote: per tutta Toscana si disse essere sentite in aria e vedute genti d’armi, sopra Arezzo, che si azzuffavano insieme

episodes.description: Before the death of Lorenzo de' Medici the elder, the cathedral of Florence was struck at its highest point by a celestial bolt with very great ruin to the building.
episodes.quote: avanti alla morte di Lorenzo de’ Medici vecchio, fu percosso il duomo nella sua più alta parte con una saetta celeste

episodes.description: Shortly before Piero Soderini, made gonfalonier for life by the Florentine people, was driven out and stripped of his rank, the palazzo was likewise struck by lightning.
episodes.quote: poco innanzi che Piero Soderini, quale era stato fatto gonfalonieri a vita dal popolo fiorentino, fosse cacciato e privo del suo grado, fu il palazzo medesimamente da uno fulgure percosso

episodes.description: Before the Gauls came to Rome, the plebeian Marcus Caedicius reported to the Senate that at midnight on the Via Nuova he had heard a more-than-human voice warning that the Gauls were coming.
episodes.quote: uno Marco Cedicio plebeio riferì al Senato avere udito di mezza notte, passando per la Via nuova, una voce, maggiore che umana

notes: Machiavelli explicitly attributes the Caedicius story to Titus Livius (Livy 5.32).

heading_en: The plebs is bold together, weak singly
thesis: The plebs united is strong, but each man by himself, thinking of his own danger, is weak: a multitude without a head is at once the most formidable and the feeblest of things.
thesis_quote: La Plebe insieme è gagliarda, di per sé è debole

propositions.statement: A multitude speaks boldly against its prince's decisions, but when punishment stares it in the face, each man, distrusting the others, runs to obey.
propositions.quote: la moltitudine è audace nel parlare, molte volte contro alle diliberazioni del loro principe; dipoi, come ei veggono la pena in viso, non si fidando l’uno dell’altro, corrono ad ubbidire

propositions.statement: Nothing is on one side more formidable than an unleashed multitude without a head, and on the other side nothing is weaker.
propositions.quote: non ci è cosa, dall’un canto, più formidabile che una moltitudine sciolta e sanza capo; e, dall’altra parte, non è cosa più debole

propositions.statement: An aroused multitude that wishes to escape these dangers must at once make from among itself a head to correct it, keep it united, and plan its defense.
propositions.quote: una moltitudine così concitata, volendo fuggire questi pericoli, ha subito a fare infra sé medesima uno capo che la corregga, tenghila unita e pensi alla sua difesa

episodes.description: After the Gallic sack many Romans moved to Veii against the Senate's ordinance; they first mocked the public edicts ordering their return under penalty, but when the deadline neared each one obeyed.
episodes.quote: comandò per i suoi editti publici che ciascuno, infra certo tempo, e sotto certe pene, tornasse a abitare a Roma

episodes.description: After the death of Virginia the Roman plebs departed from Rome and, to save itself, created twenty tribunes from among its own number.
episodes.quote: come fece la plebe romana, quando, dopo la morte di Virginia, si partì da Roma, e per salvarsi feciono infra loro venti Tribuni

notes: Quotes Livy verbatim: 'Ex ferocibus universis singuli metu suo obedientes fuere' (Livy 6.4).

heading_en: The multitude is wiser and more constant than a prince
thesis: Against the common opinion of all writers, a people that commands and is well ordered is as stable, prudent, and grateful as a prince or more so; the defects imputed to the multitude belong to all men unregulated by laws, and above all to princes.
thesis_quote: un popolo che comandi e sia bene ordinato, sarà stabile, prudente e grato non altrimenti che un principe, o meglio che un principe, eziandio stimato savio

propositions.statement: The defect writers charge to the multitude can be charged to all men individually and most of all to princes, for anyone unregulated by laws would make the same errors as an unleashed multitude.
propositions.quote: di quello difetto di che accusano gli scrittori la moltitudine, se ne possono accusare tutti gli uomini particularmente, e massime i principi; perché ciascuno, che non sia regolato dalle leggi, farebbe quelli medesimi errori che la moltitudine sciolta

propositions.statement: The variation in their conduct arises not from diverse nature but from more or less respect for the laws within which both live.
propositions.quote: la variazione del procedere loro nasce non dalla natura diversa, perché in tutti è a un modo, e, se vi è vantaggio di bene, è nel popolo; ma dallo avere più o meno rispetto alle leggi

propositions.statement: In its elections to magistracies a people chooses far better than a prince, and will never be persuaded to raise an infamous and corrupt man to dignities, as a prince easily is.
propositions.quote: Vedesi ancora, nelle sue elezioni ai magistrati, fare, di lunga, migliore elezione che un principe

propositions.statement: A licentious and tumultuous people can be spoken to by a good man and easily led back to the good way; for a bad prince there is no remedy but steel.
propositions.quote: a un popolo licenzioso e tumultuario, gli può da un uomo buono essere parlato, e facilmente può essere ridotto nella via buona: a un principe cattivo non è alcuno che possa parlare né vi è altro rimedio che il ferro

episodes.description: The Roman people condemned Manlius Capitolinus to death and shortly afterward, once no danger remained from him, supremely desired him back.
episodes.quote: come si vede aver fatto il popolo romano, di Manlio Capitolino, il quale avendo condannato a morte, sommamente dipoi desiderava quello

episodes.description: Livy describes the unleashed multitude of Syracuse after the death of Hieronymus, grandson of Hiero, which either serves humbly or dominates proudly.
episodes.quote: quando mostra gli accidenti che nacquono in Siracusa dopo la morte di Girolamo nipote di Ierone

episodes.description: Princes held wise have likewise put men to death and then supremely desired them back, as Alexander with Clitus and his other friends, and Herod with Mariamne.
episodes.quote: de’ principi, tenuti savi, i quali hanno fatto morire qualche persona, e poi sommamente desideratola: come Alessandro, Clito ed altri suoi amici; ed Erode, Marianne

episodes.description: Cities where peoples rule make excessive gains in a very short time, as Rome did after the expulsion of the kings and Athens after freeing itself from Pisistratus.
episodes.quote: come fece Roma dopo la cacciata de’ re, ed Atene da poi che la si liberò da Pisistrato

notes: Opens citing 'Tito Livio nostro' and quotes him twice verbatim; the Syracuse quotation ('Haec natura multitudinis est...') is from Livy 24.25, outside the Livy 1-10 corpus. The Rome/Athens episode spans Roman and Greek history; period set to roman-republic.

heading_en: Whose alliance is more trustworthy, a republic's or a prince's
thesis: Leagues made by force are kept by neither princes nor republics, and fear breaks both faiths alike; but where danger is urgent, and where utility tempts to betrayal, republics show somewhat more stability and keep their accords far better than princes.
thesis_quote: in questi casi, dove è il pericolo urgente, si troverrà qualche stabilità più nelle republiche, che ne’ principi

propositions.statement: Accords made by force will be observed toward you neither by a prince nor by a republic; when fear for the state comes, both will break faith and show ingratitude rather than lose it.
propositions.quote: gli accordi fatti per forza non ti saranno né da uno principe né da una republica osservati

propositions.statement: Because republics move slowly, they take longer to resolve, and therefore longer to break faith, than a prince.
propositions.quote: lo avere il moto loro tardo, farà che le perranno sempre più a risolversi che il principe, e per questo perranno più a rompere la fede di lui

propositions.statement: Confederations are broken for utility, and in this republics are far more observant of accords than princes.
propositions.quote: In questo le republiche sono, di lunga, più osservanti degli accordi, che i principi

episodes.description: Demetrius, called the besieger of cities, after conferring infinite benefits on the Athenians, was routed by his enemies and, fleeing to Athens as a friendly and obligated city, was not received by it.
episodes.quote: sendo rotto da’ suoi inimici, e rifuggendosi in Atene come in città amica ed a lui obligata, non fu ricevuto da quella

episodes.description: Pompey, routed by Caesar in Thessaly, fled to Egypt to Ptolemy, whom he had previously restored to his kingdom, and was killed by him.
episodes.quote: Pompeio, rotto che fu da Cesare in Tessaglia, si rifuggì in Egitto a Tolomeo, il quale era per lo adietro da lui stato rimesso nel regno

episodes.description: The princes of the kingdom of Naples who followed the French party awaited ruin out of loyalty, hoping for eventual restoration.
actors: princes of the kingdom of Naples
episodes.quote: sono stati quegli principi del reame di Napoli, che hanno seguite le parti franciose

episodes.description: Saguntum in Spain awaited its ruin rather than desert the Roman side.
episodes.quote: fu di questa sorte Sagunto in Ispagna, che aspettò la rovina per seguire le parti romane

episodes.description: Florence in 1512 awaited ruin for following the French party.
episodes.quote: di questa Firenze, per seguire nel 1512 le parti franciose

episodes.description: Themistocles proposed a secretly advantageous plan to the Athenians; Aristides, chosen to judge it, reported it most useful but most dishonest, and the people wholly refused it.
episodes.quote: Aristide riferì al popolo, il partito di Temistocle essere utilissimo ma disonestissimo: per la quale cosa il popolo al tutto lo ricusò

notes: The Saguntum episode (Livy 21) falls outside the Livy 1-10 corpus; no candidate given. Philip of Macedon cited as a faith-breaking prince.

heading_en: Rome gave the consulate without respect of age
thesis: Once the consulate was opened to the plebs, Rome conferred it and every other magistracy without respect of age or blood, always seeking virtue whether in young or old—a necessity for any city that wants to achieve what Rome achieved.
thesis_quote: la Republica romana, poiché il Consolato venne nella Plebe, concesse quello ai suoi cittadini sanza rispetto di età o di sangue

propositions.statement: One cannot give men hardship without reward, nor take from them the hope of attaining the reward, without danger.
propositions.quote: e’ non si può dare agli uomini disagio sanza premio, né si può tôrre loro la speranza di conseguire il premio sanza pericolo

propositions.statement: A city that does not employ its plebs in anything glorious may treat it as it pleases, but one that wants to do what Rome did cannot make this distinction.
propositions.quote: la città che non adopera la sua plebe a alcuna cosa gloriosa, la può trattare a suo modo

propositions.statement: When a young man has shown notable virtue, it would be most harmful for the city not to avail itself of him then, waiting for the vigor of mind of that age to grow old with him.
propositions.quote: sarebbe cosa dannosissima che la città non se ne potessi valere allora, e che l’avesse a aspettare che fosse invecchiato con lui quel vigore dell’animo

episodes.description: Valerius Corvinus was made consul at twenty-three, and told his soldiers that the consulate was the reward of virtue, not of blood.
episodes.quote: si vede per il testimone di Valerio Corvino, che fu fatto Consolo in ventitré anni

episodes.description: Rome availed itself of Valerius Corvinus, Scipio, Pompey, and many others who triumphed very young.
episodes.quote: come si valse Roma di Valerio Corvino, di Scipione e di Pompeio, e di molti altri, che trionfarono giovanissimi

notes: Latin tag «praemium virtutis, non sanguinis» echoes Valerius Corvus' speech in Livy 7.32; the consulship at 23 is narrated at Livy 7.26.
